hook.text: Dry, rubbery chicken breast? It's not you. It's the method. Here are seven steps to chicken that is juicy, tender and safe, every single time. And stay for step six: it's the one that ends the guessing for good.

intro.text: Chicken breast has almost no fat, so there is very little margin. Two things dry it out: uneven thickness, and cooking it too long. We'll fix both, then add a quick salt brine for extra moisture, and a thermometer, the only reliable way to know it's done.

youneed.text: You'll need boneless chicken breasts, salt and pepper, a skillet with a lid, a meat thermometer, and a meat mallet or a rolling pin. Plus a little oil.

step-1.text: Step one. Place the chicken breast between two sheets of plastic wrap or baking paper on a cutting board. Using a mallet, a rolling pin or the bottom of a heavy pan, gently pound the thickest part until the whole breast is about three quarters of an inch, or two centimetres, thick. Don't pound it into a pancake, because you just want an even shape. Equal thickness means the whole piece cooks at the same speed, which is the key to juicy results. Very large breasts can also be cut in half horizontally to make two thinner cutlets, which cook faster.

step-2.text: Step two. Dissolve two tablespoons of salt in four cups, or one litre, of cold water. Put the chicken in the water, and leave it for thirty minutes in the fridge. The salt helps the meat hold on to more moisture while it cooks. If you're short of time, skip the brine, and instead salt the chicken generously on both sides fifteen minutes before cooking. Don't brine for more than an hour, or the texture can turn spongy. Raw chicken must always stay in the fridge. Always use a clean bowl and wash it afterward with hot soapy water, since raw chicken juices carry bacteria.

step-3.text: Step three. Remove the chicken from the brine and pat it very dry with paper towels. Dry meat browns, wet meat steams. Don't rinse raw chicken under the tap, because that splashes bacteria around your sink. Brush each side with a teaspoon of oil, and season with pepper, paprika, garlic powder or any dry spices you like. If you skipped the brine, add salt now. Wash your hands and the board with hot soapy water afterward. Smoked paprika, garlic powder and dried thyme make an easy all-purpose rub, with no sugar to burn in the pan.

step-4.text: Step four. Heat a skillet over medium-high heat for two minutes, then add a thin layer of oil. When it shimmers, lay the chicken in the pan, presentation side down. It should sizzle right away. Leave it alone for five to six minutes without moving it, until the underside is a deep golden brown. Don't crowd the pan. If you're cooking more than two breasts, work in batches. That browned crust is where the flavor comes from. If the pan smokes heavily, lower the heat slightly. A deep golden color is what you want, not black.

step-5.text: Step five. Flip the chicken with tongs, then turn the heat down to medium-low and cover the pan with a lid. The trapped steam finishes the cooking gently, so the center cooks through without the outside burning. Cook for another five to seven minutes, depending on thickness. Don't keep lifting the lid, because the heat escapes. A gentle finish is the difference between juicy and dry chicken, so be patient and keep the heat low. If your breasts are very thin, three to four minutes will be enough, so start checking early.

step-6.text: Step six. Don't guess. Push an instant-read thermometer into the thickest part of the breast, without touching the pan. Chicken is safe to eat at 165 degrees Fahrenheit, or 74 Celsius. Take the chicken out of the pan once it reaches that temperature, because it keeps cooking a little as it rests. If it's below 165, cover the pan, and cook for a minute or two more, then check again. Cutting into it to look is not reliable, and it lets the juices escape. Check a second breast as well if you are cooking several, because they never finish at exactly the same time.

step-7.text: Step seven. Move the chicken to a clean board or plate, and let it rest for five to ten minutes. The juices relax and spread back through the meat, instead of running out when you cut. Cover loosely with foil if your kitchen is cool. Then slice across the grain, in slices about half an inch thick. Serve in a salad, a sandwich or with vegetables. Store leftovers in the fridge within two hours, and eat within three to four days. Try the sliced chicken over a salad or inside a wrap for an easy lunch the next day.

step-8.text: If the chicken came out dry, you can still save dinner. Slice it thinly, and warm it for a minute in broth. You can also shred it for tacos or soup. If the center is pink, do not guess. Pink can be safe, and white can be raw, so trust only the thermometer. If it reads below 165 degrees Fahrenheit, return it to the pan.

step-9.text: A thermometer is only useful if it is accurate. Test it in a glass of ice water: it should read 32 degrees Fahrenheit, or 0 Celsius. If it is off by a few degrees, adjust it if you can, or replace it. Slide the tip into the thickest part, away from the pan. Wait until the number stops moving. Wash the probe with hot soapy water after each use.

step-10.text: Spread the chicken in a shallow container so it cools quickly, then cover it and refrigerate. For longer storage, freeze it, and thaw it overnight in the fridge, never on the counter. Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot all the way through, or 165 degrees Fahrenheit again. Add a splash of water or broth, and cover the dish, so the meat stays tender.

mistakes.text: Here are the mistakes to avoid. First, cooking a thick, uneven breast. The thin part dries out before the thick part is safe. Even it out first. Second, cooking without a thermometer. Overcooking by only a few minutes can ruin the texture, and undercooking is unsafe. And third, slicing right away. Resting keeps the juices where they belong. Do these three things right, and your chicken will be tender every time. Keep it simple, trust the thermometer, and enjoy the result.

recap.text: Let's recap. Even out the thickness. Brine for moisture. Dry and season well. Sear in a hot pan. Flip, cover and lower the heat. Check with a thermometer for 165 degrees. And rest the chicken, then slice across the grain. Seven steps, about thirty minutes of cooking, and chicken breast that stays juicy. Bonus sections cover rescuing dry or pink chicken, checking your thermometer, and storing leftovers safely.

outro.text: That's how you cook chicken breast without drying it out. If dinner was juicy tonight, subscribe to WikiTube, because we publish a new how-to every single day. Tell us in the comments how you season your chicken, and what you would like us to explain next. See you tomorrow. Next time, try different spices, because the method stays exactly the same.

short-hook.text: Dry chicken breast every time? It's uneven thickness and guesswork. Fix both.

short-step-1.text: One. Pound the thick end until the breast is an even thickness, then dry and season it.

short-step-2.text: Two. Sear in a hot pan for five minutes, flip, cover, and cook on low.

short-step-3.text: Three. Take it out at 165 degrees Fahrenheit, 74 Celsius, and rest it for five minutes.

short2-hook.text: Stop rinsing raw chicken under the tap.

short2-beat-1.text: Rinsing raw chicken under the tap splashes bacteria around your sink.

short2-beat-2.text: Pat it very dry with paper towels, then wash your hands and the board with hot soapy water.
